title: Four places
hookLine: the places of the birth, awakening, first sermon and passing, worth seeing with devotion
last: SET THE WORDS BESIDE THE DISCOURSES.

cards: The Buddha is lying between the twin sal trees at Kusinara now, near the end. And Ananda raises a practical worry.

Until now, he says, at the end of every rainy season, monks from all over came to see the Blessed One, and we got to see them, and learn from them. When you're gone, we won't have that. Where will people go?
Underneath it sits a plainer question: where do we go now, to feel close? The Buddha's answer is very concrete.

teach.b: There are four places, Ananda, that a person of faith should see, places that stir the heart. The Pali word is samvejaniya: stirring, moving.
The first: here the Tathagata was born. The second: here the Tathagata awakened to full awakening. The third: here the Tathagata set the wheel of the Dhamma rolling.
The fourth: here the Tathagata passed into final nibbana. The sutta itself doesn't name the towns.
It simply says here, here, here, here.
Tradition has filled in the map: Lumbini, in what is now Nepal; Bodh Gaya, under the tree; the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi, now called Sarnath; and Kusinara, where he is lying as he speaks.

Then he adds that monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen, will come to these places, and whoever dies on such a pilgrimage with a heart at peace will be reborn in a good destination. It's a startling moment.
A teacher who spent his life pointing people inward, to the breath and the mind, also says: go and stand there.
The places don't hold magic in the text. They hold the four turning points of one life: arriving, waking up, sharing it, letting go. Pilgrims still travel between them.

how: Buddhists from across Asia and the world make pilgrimage to Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar, often visiting all four on one journey, chanting, meditating and making offerings at each.

o: four shrines that hold the Buddha's relics today
his birth, awakening, first teaching and passing
the four cities where the Buddha spent the rains

p: where the wheel was set rolling

s: DN 16 names Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kusinara by name
the sutta says only 'here the Tathagata was born', and so on; tradition supplies the names.
samvejaniya means something like stirring or moving
places that shake the heart awake.
Ananda's question was about where monks would go once the Buddha was gone
they used to come see him after the rains.

games.q: you're Ananda. your teacher is dying. you worry that people will have nowhere to go to feel close to him. what does he tell you?
o: visit four places: his birth, awakening, first teaching and passing.
build one great temple in his name.
games.why: he names four places worth seeing with devotion, places that stir the heart.

practice: Picture the four places one at a time, a few breaths each: a grove where a child is born, a tree where a man sits until he understands, a deer park where five friends listen, two sal trees where an old man lies down.
Then, if you like, picture four places in your own life: where you began, where something woke up in you, where you first shared it, and where you let something go.

wordCard.voice: Four places. Birth, awakening, the first teaching and the final passing: the four places the Buddha said are worth seeing, places that stir the heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samvejaniya: stirring, moving. the four places are samvejaniya thana, places that stir.

carryVoice: Your line: places that stir the heart. Born, awakened, taught, passed: one life's four turning points. That's day five hundred forty-nine.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the four places that stir the heart
